parts.note: a suit-presser sounds like a tailor with an iron, but here he is a suitor pressing his suit of love, and his craft is both his skill and a vessel (a ship)

explanation.surface: A question about the trade skill of someone who irons suits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suit' is a proposal of marriage, so the presser is a wooer; 'craft' then hints at a boat, which the answer's last four letters supply.
explanation.definitionFit: Wooing is the art of pressing one's suit, and the word ends in a vessel's name, matching 'craft'.

explanation.surface: A bird wearing clothes suitable for going outside.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition splits the word as 'cap on', ready to go out.
explanation.definitionFit: A capon is a castrated cockerel fattened for the table; someone with headgear on is ready to go out.

annotationWithheld.why: 'Waves unseat Lud (9)' as printed: the wordplay is an anagram of UNSEAT LUD with no word signalling the anagram (old-style clue), so no indicator can be named.

clue.text: This kind of lay can be made in 69 ways, said Kipling

definitions.text: This kind of lay can be made in 69 ways, said Kipling

parts.words: This kind of lay can be made in 69 ways, said Kipling
parts.note: Kipling wrote that there are nine and sixty ways of constructing a certain kind of song, and every single one is right

explanation.surface: A remark about poems that Kipling said could be composed in many ways.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's 'In the Neolithic Age': 'There are nine and sixty ways of constructing tribal lays, And every single one of them is right!' A lay is a ballad.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's line names the kind of ballad belonging to a clan or tribe.

parts.note: the French author whose first name is Victor wrote the novel Quatre-vingt-treize, Ninety-Three

explanation.surface: A champion from the year 1793.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Victor' looks like a winner but is the first name of the author of the novel Ninety-Three (Quatre-vingt-treize), set in 1793.
explanation.definitionFit: Victor Hugo wrote the French Revolution novel titled Ninety-Three.

parts.note: a hairdresser's perm, short for permanent wave, is artificially produced and its quality is lasting

explanation.surface: A property of a sea wave made by artificial means.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wave' suggests the sea, but a perm is a 'permanent wave' put into hair; its defining quality is lasting.
explanation.definitionFit: The quality of lasting is what a permanent wave in hair is named for.

parts.note: a lozenge here is the diamond shape of geometry and heraldry, not a cough sweet, hence inedible

explanation.surface: A throat sweet that cannot be eaten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lozenge' suggests a sweet; 'Inedible' tells you it is the four-sided figure instead.
explanation.definitionFit: The geometric figure with four equal sides and oblique angles is called a lozenge or diamond shape.

clue.text: It carries weight with footmen abroad

definitions.text: It carries weight with footmen abroad

parts.words: It carries weight with footmen abroad
parts.note: footmen are walkers rather than servants, and the bag they carry has a German name, hence abroad

explanation.surface: Something that is influential with servants overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carries weight' suggests influence and 'footmen' servants; really it is a hiker's pack, from German Rucken (back) and Sack.
explanation.definitionFit: A hiker's backpack carries a load for walkers, and its name comes from German.

clue.text: The Primate gives a tortured groan

indicators.note: a tortured thing is twisted out of shape, so these letters are bent into another order

explanation.surface: An archbishop lets out a pained groan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Primate' suggests an archbishop, but it is the ape, short for orang-utan; 'tortured' rearranges GROAN.
explanation.definitionFit: The orang-utan, often shortened, is a great ape and so a primate.

clue.text: Room for one without a chair ?

definitions.text: Room for one without a chair ?

parts.words: Room for one without a chair ?
parts.note: a single room where you sit on the bed because there is nowhere else to sit

explanation.surface: A question about where a person with no seat should go.
explanation.walkthrough: A one-room flat with a bed that doubles as seating, so a lodger without a chair sits on the bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedsit is a single room for sleeping and living in, where the bed serves as a seat.

clue.text: It's up to the consumer to prove it!

definitions.text: It's up to the consumer to prove it!

parts.words: It's up to the consumer to prove it!
parts.note: refers to the proverb that the proof of this dessert is in the eating, so the eater does the proving

explanation.surface: A slogan saying the customer must test the product.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'the proof of the pudding is in the eating' means you judge a thing by trying it, so the consumer is the one who proves it.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb names this dish as the thing proved by eating, so the eater tests it.

parts.note: Hotspur in Shakespeare's Henry IV Part 1 speaks of putting down the deposed king as 'that sweet lovely rose'

explanation.surface: A quotation from Shakespeare's fiery rebel praising a flower.
explanation.walkthrough: In Henry IV Part 1 Hotspur says 'To put down Richard, that sweet lovely rose'; the rose is the deposed King Richard II.
explanation.definitionFit: The Shakespearean quotation refers to King Richard II by that flower image.

clue.text: Invalid? Ah, take a course of Indian waters

parts.note: something invalid in law is null, void
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sick person sighs and is sent on a cruise along Indian rivers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Invalid?' looks like a sick person, but it is the adjective: legally void.
explanation.definitionFit: A nullah in India is a riverbed or ravine through which water runs in the rains, a watercourse.

clue.text: A florin, for example, first class for an unfriendly throw

parts.note: a florin was the old British two-shilling coin, and S is the abbreviation for a shilling, so two of them
A1 is first class, read as the letters AI

explanation.surface: A coin given as an example of top quality, then thrown in anger.
explanation.walkthrough: The florin was a British coin worth two shillings (2s), so it gives SS; A1 means first class.
explanation.definitionFit: An assegai is a slender spear of southern Africa, thrown at an enemy.

parts.note: an old-fashioned literary word for dressed or attired

explanation.definitionFit: The old literary word for dressed comes from apparel, meaning clothing.

indicators.note: 'Sound' at the start tells us the word for conservative is to be heard, not spelt

parts.note: in politics the conservative side is the right

explanation.surface: A sensible conservative way of doing things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' looks like an adjective meaning sensible but is the signal that RIGHT is heard as a word with another spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A rite is a set ceremony, a prescribed form of religious or formal observance.

clue.text: Obscure engineer opposed to change of diet

parts.note: RE, the Royal Engineers, gives an engineer
con, as in pros and cons, means against

indicators.note: a change of the letters of the following word rearranges them

explanation.surface: A gloomy engineer who refuses to alter what he eats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change of' rearranges DIET into DITE; RE is the Royal Engineers, a British Army corps.
explanation.definitionFit: Recondite knowledge is abstruse, little known and hard to grasp.

explanation.surface: A gated area at the top reserved for the elite.
explanation.walkthrough: The top pastry casing of a pie encloses the filling; the same phrase is slang for the social elite.
explanation.definitionFit: The pastry lid seals a pie at the top, and the phrase also means the aristocracy or social elite.

indicators.note: 'into' signals turning the letters of push and Diana into something else, a new word

explanation.surface: An instruction to shove someone named Diana into ancient Indian literature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' turns PUSH DIANA into the answer by rearranging its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Upanishads are ancient philosophical texts of Hinduism, written in Sanskrit.

indicators.note: an arrangement puts the letters of 'a built-on' in a new order

explanation.surface: An extension added to a house for bathing facilities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arrangement' rearranges A BUILT-ON; the surface is a bathroom extension.
explanation.definitionFit: An ablution is a ritual or ordinary act of washing oneself.

clue.text: White House lad in a hot spot at sea

definitions.text: lad in a hot spot at sea

explanation.surface: A boy from the presidential residence in danger on the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: The Moroccan port's name is Spanish for 'white house'. The second half points to Casabianca, the boy who 'stood on the burning deck' in Hemans's poem, a name one letter away.
explanation.definitionFit: Spanish casa means house and blanca white; the burning-deck boy of the poem has a near-identical name.

clue.text: Not given to cheating like Tennyson's Elaine

explanation.surface: An honest player compared to a heroine of Tennyson.
explanation.walkthrough: In Tennyson's Idylls of the King she is 'Elaine the fair'.
explanation.definitionFit: Honest dealing is just and even-handed; Tennyson's Elaine is called beautiful, the old sense of the word.

clue.text: Unruffled, that is, like an old China hand

parts.note: someone unruffled stays calm, cool
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, 'that is'

explanation.surface: Calm, like an experienced expatriate in China.
explanation.walkthrough: An 'old China hand' usually means a veteran expatriate; here 'hand' is a labourer, the old term for an unskilled worker in China.
explanation.definitionFit: The old term for an Asian manual labourer, a hired hand, especially in China.

clue.text: Acknowledge his authority when crossing the main line

definitions.text: Acknowledge his authority when crossing the main line

parts.words: Acknowledge his authority when crossing the main line
parts.note: the main is the sea and the line the equator; sailors crossing it perform a ceremony honouring the sea god

explanation.surface: Advice to respect someone in charge when you cross a busy railway line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main line' suggests railways, but the main is the sea and the line is the equator, where the line-crossing ceremony honours the Roman sea god.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman god of the sea presides over the equator-crossing ritual on ships.

explanation.surface: Someone stared in wonder, resembling a man named Paul.
explanation.walkthrough: Paul Pry is the nosy title character of John Poole's 1825 comedy, so 'like Paul' is Pry-ed.
explanation.definitionFit: To peer nosily into others' affairs is to snoop; and Paul Pry, the stage busybody, gives his surname.

parts.note: the rugby referee's call ending a game, which can also read as 'without swagger'

explanation.surface: A game that ended quietly and without fuss.
explanation.walkthrough: In rugby the referee's call 'no side' ends the match; 'side' also means airs and graces, so having none is being modest.
explanation.definitionFit: The rugby term for full time also reads as lacking pretension, which is modesty.

clue.text: Stopped a hundred short, and relaxed

indicators.note: being short of something means lacking it, so the hundred is taken away

parts.note: to stop is to cease
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: A batsman stopped before reaching his century and then relaxed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' removes C from CEASED; the surface is a cricketer out short of a hundred.
explanation.definitionFit: To ease off is to slacken or loosen, so relaxed is a synonym.

parts.note: MO, medical officer, is a medicine man, with the 's giving S

explanation.surface: A doctor who also takes bets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bookmaker' suggests a betting shop, but it is the prophet who gives his name to a book of the Old Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: Amos is a prophet whose name is the title of an Old Testament book, so its maker.

annotationWithheld.why: 'First I nail it ! (7)' as printed: the wordplay is an anagram of I NAIL IT with no word signalling the anagram (old-style clue), so no indicator can be named.

indicators.note: the invoice formula 'errors and omissions excepted' is read as 'E and O excepted', so those letters are left out

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An economist associated with a brewery building, with the usual invoice disclaimer.
explanation.walkthrough: E.&O.E., printed on invoices for 'errors and omissions excepted', is read as 'E and O excepted': drop the O and the E from MALTHOUSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Malthus was the English economist known for his theory of population growth.

clue.text: Port for many in the garden

indicators.note: the letter for 'many' goes inside the word for the garden

parts.note: the Garden of Eden in Genesis
M, the Roman numeral for a thousand, stands for many

explanation.surface: A drink served to lots of people in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' could be the drink, but it is the German harbour town.
explanation.definitionFit: Emden is a harbour town in north-west Germany on the Ems estuary.

parts.note: climbing down a tree and being born into a later generation of a lineage

explanation.surface: Someone climbing down a tree that belongs to the family.
explanation.walkthrough: The picture is of climbing down a real tree; the sense is of being born into a line of ancestry.
explanation.definitionFit: To be of a lineage is to come down from ancestors, and the word also means simply went lower.
